opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the first thing I'd say is: don't treat distillation as a solved, one-size-fits-all recipe. A lot of people still default to the classic setup, where you take a teacher, generate a fixed dataset of outputs, and fine-tune the student on it with a forward KL or plain cross-entropy loss. That works, but it leaves a lot on the table.

One thing we found in our work on on-policy distillation is that the mismatch between what the student sees during training and what it actually generates at inference time matters a lot. If the student is only ever trained on teacher-generated sequences, then at test time it drifts into states the teacher never showed it, and errors compound. So letting the student generate its own outputs and having the teacher give feedback on those is often a cheap, big win. My advice would be to try that early, because it's usually not much harder to implement than standard supervised distillation.

The second thing is to actually play with the divergence. Forward KL tends to make the student mode-covering, spreading probability mass to cover everything the teacher might say, which can hurt when the student is much smaller. Reverse KL, or something in between like a generalized Jensen-Shannon, can be more mode-seeking and give you sharper, higher-quality outputs. Which one is best really depends on the task. For something like summarization, where diversity matters less, you might prefer one; for open-ended generation, another. So I'd treat it as a hyperparameter rather than a fixed choice.

Third, think about how distillation composes with whatever else you're doing. If you're also doing RL fine-tuning, you can often fold the distillation signal in as a reward or a regularizer, rather than running them as separate stages. That tends to be more compute-efficient and keeps the student from forgetting what it got from the teacher.

And practically, start small. Pick a student and teacher pair where you can iterate quickly, measure on held-out tasks that reflect what you actually care about, not just perplexity, and look at the generations yourself. A lot of the differences between these methods only show up when you read the samples. Once you've found something that works at small scale, it usually transfers reasonably well when you scale up.

r001.rationale: The response says on-policy distillation is usually not much harder to implement than supervised distillation and discusses combining distillation with RL fine-tuning. It does not explain that newer methods are easy to try because they fit practitioners’ existing reinforcement-learning infrastructure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd say is: don't start with the fancy method. Start with the baseline that's embarrassingly simple. If you're distilling a big model into a small one, just do the standard thing first, generate samples from the teacher, do supervised fine-tuning on the student, and get a really solid number on your eval. A surprising amount of the time, that baseline is much stronger than people expect, and if you don't have it nailed down, you have no idea whether your new on-policy or reverse-KL variant is actually buying you anything or whether you just tuned the learning rate better on the second run.

The second thing is to be honest about what the student is for. Distillation in the literature is usually framed as "match the teacher," but in practice you usually have a narrower target. Maybe you care about math reasoning, or you care about a specific coding setup, or you care about long-context behavior. The newer methods, especially the on-policy ones where the student generates its own outputs and the teacher gives feedback on them, tend to shine exactly when the gap between teacher and student is large and the student is making mistakes the teacher never would. So if your student is already decent on the task, the gains from going on-policy might be small. If it's really struggling, that's where I'd expect the bigger win, because you're training on the student's actual failure modes rather than on the teacher's clean trajectories it can't reproduce anyway.

Third, and this is the one people underestimate: the data matters more than the loss. Where are your prompts coming from? Are they in-distribution for what you'll see at deployment? Are you deduplicating against your eval? I've seen a lot of "method X beats method Y" results that completely flip when you change the prompt set. So I'd spend as much time on the prompt distribution as on the algorithm.

And then practically, keep the experiments cheap. Use a small student, a mid-sized teacher, and a fast eval loop. The point of the early experiments isn't to get the best number, it's to learn which knobs matter. Does the KL direction matter for your task? Does mixing in some teacher-generated data with on-policy data help? Does temperature when sampling from the student matter? Those questions you can answer at small scale, and then you scale up the thing that worked. If you only ever run the full-scale version, you'll run three experiments and have no idea why any of them did what they did.

The last thing I'd say is to look at the outputs. Really read them. Distillation losses can go down while the student learns to mimic surface patterns of the teacher, like formatting and verbosity, without actually getting better at the underlying task. The eval will usually catch it eventually, but reading samples catches it a week earlier.

r001.rationale: The response recommends trying newer distillation methods through small, cheap experiments, but does not say they are easy to try because they fit practitioners’ existing reinforcement-learning infrastructure.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with the problem you’re trying to solve. Are you trying to make the model cheaper to serve, reduce latency, or preserve a particular capability in a smaller model? That determines what a useful experiment looks like.

Then establish a simple baseline and a good evaluation set. Before adding complexity, check whether the student can learn from the teacher’s outputs on representative examples. From there, change one thing at a time—the data, the training objective, or how you get feedback from the teacher—so you can tell what actually helps.

I’d also pay attention to where the student fails. A method can improve an aggregate score while still missing the cases your users care about. Treat newer methods as hypotheses to test in your setting, and compare the gains against the extra training cost and complexity.

r001.rationale: The response recommends testing newer distillation methods in a practitioner’s setting, but does not say they are easy to try because they fit existing reinforcement-learning infrastructure.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start with a concrete question: what are you trying to improve? Is it the quality of a smaller model, inference cost, or performance on a particular task? That determines what a useful distillation experiment looks like.

Then build a simple baseline and a good evaluation loop. Before adding a more sophisticated method, try distilling from teacher-generated responses and see where the student struggles. Are the responses incorrect, too difficult for the student, or different from what it will encounter in production? Those failure modes can tell you more than an aggregate benchmark score.

For newer methods, I’d keep the initial experiments small and change one thing at a time. Compare under similar compute and data budgets, and include the cost of generating the training data. You want to understand whether the method helps in your setting and why, so you can make an informed decision about scaling it up.

r001.rationale: The response recommends small, controlled experiments and evaluation, but does not say newer distillation methods are easy to try because they fit practitioners’ existing reinforcement-learning infrastructure.
